title: Why Muslims Believe Jesus Is Alive and Will Return
summary: Islamic teaching on Jesus' second coming — a genuine point of overlap with Christian eschatology, alongside real differences in what his return is expected to mean.

body.text: A surprising overlap: both faiths expect Jesus to return

Following on from the previous lesson: since Islam holds that God raised Jesus to Himself rather than allowing him to die on the cross, mainstream Islamic teaching also holds that Jesus is alive right now, and will return to earth before the Day of Judgment — a belief with real, genuine overlap with Christian expectation of Christ's second coming, even though what happens around that return is understood quite differently.
What Islamic tradition says Jesus will do

Hadith literature describes Jesus returning to defeat a figure called the Dajjal (a deceiving, false-messiah-like figure with real parallels to the Christian Antichrist), to establish justice on earth, and — significantly — to affirm Islam rather than to found or reaffirm Christianity as a separate religion, since Islamic teaching holds there is ultimately one true religion taught by every prophet, corrected and completed with Muhammad.

Christian eschatology generally centers Christ's return as the climactic event of all history, tied directly to his identity as divine Savior and Judge. Islamic eschatology includes Jesus' return as one significant sign among several leading up to the Day of Judgment, but the ultimate Judge in Islamic theology is Allah alone — Jesus returns as a prophet and servant fulfilling a specific role, not as a divine judge presiding over humanity in his own right.

This shared expectation — that Jesus is alive and will return — is one of the more concrete, usable bridges in this whole collection when talking with Christian family, since it directly counters any impression that Islam simply dismisses Jesus as a finished, past figure. It's worth pairing honestly with the real differences in what that return is expected to accomplish, rather than overstating the overlap.

body.question: Will Jesus's return convert everyone to Islam, according to Islamic teaching?
body.answer: Islamic eschatology generally describes Jesus' return as leading to widespread recognition of the truth of Islam and a period of justice and peace, though specific hadith accounts vary in detail and this remains a matter of eschatological belief rather than something that can be independently verified — the same is true, of course, of Christian expectations around the second coming.

body.question: Is the "Dajjal" in Islam the same figure as the Christian Antichrist?
body.answer: The two figures share real, recognisable parallels — a deceptive, false-messiah figure who appears before the end times — and some scholars of comparative religion treat them as closely related concepts, though the two traditions describe the figure's specific characteristics and the surrounding events somewhat differently.
